title: Medically Tailored Meals Cut Hospitalisations by 31 Per Cent. For the Diaspora, This Is More Than Vindication.
excerpt: The largest Medicaid study on 'food is medicine' just proved what South Asian kitchens have practised for centuries. Now the healthcare system is catching up.
body:
The phrase your grandmother never said out loud — because she never had to — just landed in *Nature Medicine* with a dataset behind it.

Researchers at Tufts University, UMass Chan Medical School, and Community Servings published the largest-ever statewide Medicaid analysis of medically tailored meals this month, and the numbers are difficult to argue with. Massachusetts Medicaid members who received dietitian-designed, condition-specific home-delivered meals experienced 31 per cent fewer hospitalisations and 20 per cent fewer emergency department visits than a matched comparison group who qualified but did not enrol.

The per-person healthcare savings: $3,433 over an average of roughly six months on the programme — offsetting 98 per cent of its cost.

"Our results show that food really is medicine, with major clinical and policy implications for health-insurance coverage of medically tailored meals," said Dariush Mozaffarian, cardiologist and director of the Food is Medicine Institute at Tufts, who led the study.

The findings arrive at a moment when America's medical establishment is simultaneously admitting how little it knows about nutrition. The average medical student in the United States receives 1.2 hours of nutrition education across four years of training. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced this week that 19 more medical schools have pledged to require at least 40 hours of nutrition education for students starting in autumn 2026, bringing the total to 73. Eight major accrediting bodies — including the National Board of Medical Examiners and the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education — have committed to strengthening nutrition training across residency programmes.

It is a staggering admission. For decades, the system that prescribed statins and insulin to manage diet-related disease was itself untrained in diet.

## What Medically Tailored Meals Actually Are

These are not Meals on Wheels. Medically tailored meals are designed by registered dietitians for specific conditions — diabetes, heart failure, cancer, chronic kidney disease, depression — and prepared by accredited providers. The Tufts study tracked 1,866 adults across 11 Accountable Care Organisations in Massachusetts against 1,372 matched adults who met the same eligibility criteria but did not receive meals.

The programme's power lies in precision: meals are prescribed based on clinical assessment, not generic dietary guidelines. Each patient's box is different.

"As Medicaid programmes across the country build nutrition into care, holding to these standards is what will determine whether food is medicine delivers on its promise," said Alissa Wassung, executive director of the Food is Medicine Coalition.

At least a dozen US states are now piloting medically tailored meal programmes through Medicaid, serving the 71 million Americans who qualify.

## The South Asian Dimension Is Personal

South Asians in the US, UK, and Canada carry a disproportionate burden of exactly the conditions this programme targets. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among South Asian Americans is roughly four times the national average. Cardiovascular disease strikes a decade earlier. Fatty liver disease is endemic even at lower BMI thresholds.

And yet the diaspora's own food tradition — turmeric-laced dals, vegetable-heavy thalis, fermented rice, bitter gourd, fenugreek — is one of the world's oldest food-as-medicine systems. Ayurveda codified the link between diet and disease thousands of years before a Tufts researcher published it in *Nature Medicine*.

The irony is not lost on anyone paying attention. A healthcare system that spent decades telling South Asian immigrants their food was too oily, too spicy, too carb-heavy is now institutionalising the principle those kitchens were built on.

The difference is rigour. The medically tailored meal model takes the intuition and wraps it in clinical evidence, dietitian oversight, and measurable outcomes. It is not a rejection of the desi kitchen. It is a validation — with a prescription pad attached.

## What Comes Next

A separate study presented at the American Diabetes Association's conference this month by Abbott and the Public Health Institute showed that participants in a food-based intervention paired with community health worker coaching doubled their daily vegetable intake, nearly doubled fruit consumption, and saw medication adherence rise from 57 to 94 per cent.

The policy trajectory is clear. Kennedy's nutrition education push, the Medicaid meal pilots, and the ADA-presented data all point in the same direction: the most powerful drug in the chronic disease arsenal may be the one that never required a prescription.

For NRIs watching from abroad — many of whom navigate two food cultures, two healthcare systems, and two sets of dietary advice — the message is overdue. The science finally matches the plate.

*Sources: Nature Medicine (Tufts/UMass Chan/Community Servings, June 2026); HHS announcement on medical school nutrition education pledge (June 9, 2026); Abbott/Public Health Institute study at ADA 86th Scientific Sessions (June 2026)*
